project.name: Quarterly Configuration Audit — CI Sweep
project.description: Five configuration items, five approved baselines, one question for each: does what's actually running still match what was signed off? Before this quarter's audit closes, you need to check each one against its recorded baseline - not by trusting whatever a tag currently points to, but by comparing against what was actually approved.

start.speaker: Narrator
start.narrative: Five configuration items, five baselines, one quarterly audit to close out. You decide to check each one against its recorded baseline before signing off - one at a time, comparing actual commits, not just trusting a tag's current position.

check-nova-api.speaker: You
check-nova-api.narrative: CI 1 of 5: Nova API. Its last approved baseline, BL-01, was tagged at a specific commit - "chore: tag baseline BL-01 - approved launch configuration." Since then, one more commit landed: a rate-limit threshold bump, referencing CR-201. Nothing about it looks suspicious - signed, reasonable, with a real CR reference.

a2.message: chore: tag baseline BL-01 - approved launch configuration

a3.message: fix: bump rate-limit threshold under load (Refs: CR-201)

check-nova-api.prompt: Does Nova API's prod still match its approved baseline?

choices.label: No - prod has a commit on top of BL-01 that was never itself audited
Yes - it's signed, reasonable, and references a real CR

api-pushback.speaker: Sana
api-pushback.narrative: "Signed and reasonable isn't the same as audited, though. Did you actually compare prod's commit ID against BL-01's, or just judge the change on its own merits?"

api-escalate.speaker: You
api-escalate.narrative: You judged whether the change itself looked fine, not whether it matched what was actually approved - those are different questions.
api-escalate.prompt: Do you compare the commit IDs directly, or defend your answer?

choices.label: Compare BL-01's and prod's commit IDs directly
Defend it - the change itself is fine

api-recover.speaker: You
api-recover.narrative: You compare the IDs directly. BL-01 names one commit; prod names a different one, one step ahead. A reasonable-looking change is still an unaudited one.

api-worse.speaker: Narrator
api-worse.narrative: You sign off on Nova API as matching its baseline. The rate-limit change - never itself reviewed against a new baseline - stays permanently unaudited, treated as "basically part of BL-01" from now on.

api-bad-ending.speaker: Narrator
api-bad-ending.narrative: Months later, an incident traces back to that same rate-limit threshold - and the postmortem discovers it was never actually audited, because the last review certified prod as "unchanged since BL-01."

ending.debrief: "The change looks reasonable" was never the question - "does it match what was actually approved" was. Prod sat one unaudited commit past BL-01 for the whole quarter because a sensible-looking diff got waved through instead of compared against the baseline's real commit ID.

check-nova-web.speaker: You
check-nova-web.narrative: CI 2 of 5: Nova Web. Its baseline, BL-04, is tagged directly at prod's current commit.

w2.message: chore: tag baseline BL-04 - approved web configuration

check-nova-web.prompt: Does Nova Web's prod still match its approved baseline?

choices.label: Yes - prod's commit ID is exactly BL-04's
No - can't be sure without comparing again

web-flag-note.speaker: Narrator
web-flag-note.narrative: You compare again anyway. They match exactly - same commit ID.

check-nova-worker.speaker: You
check-nova-worker.narrative: CI 3 of 5: Nova Worker. Its baseline, BL-02, includes a retry-cap fix on top of the original retry logic. But prod's ref points further back - before that fix ever landed.

n1.message: feat: add retry logic for failed jobs

n2.message: fix: cap retry attempts at 3 to avoid infinite loop

n3.message: chore: tag baseline BL-02 - approved worker configuration

check-nova-worker.prompt: Does Nova Worker's prod still match its approved baseline?

choices.label: No - prod is missing the retry-cap fix that BL-02 included
Yes - it's the same retry logic, close enough

worker-pushback.speaker: Sana
worker-pushback.narrative: "Close enough? BL-02 exists specifically because that unbounded retry logic caused an infinite loop. If prod's missing the cap, that's not a minor gap."

worker-escalate.speaker: You
worker-escalate.narrative: You treated "same feature, roughly" as compliant instead of checking whether prod actually includes everything the baseline does.
worker-escalate.prompt: Do you check what BL-02 actually included, or defend it as close enough?

choices.label: Defend it - it's fundamentally the same retry logic

worker-recover.speaker: You
worker-recover.narrative: You check properly. BL-02 is the retry-cap commit; prod is one commit before it. Prod is missing exactly the fix the baseline exists to guarantee.

worker-worse.speaker: Narrator
worker-worse.narrative: You sign off on Nova Worker as compliant. The uncapped retry logic stays live in production, believed to be safely covered by an audit that never actually checked for the fix.

worker-bad-ending.speaker: Narrator
worker-bad-ending.narrative: A failed job triggers the exact infinite retry loop BL-02 was created to prevent, taking down the worker fleet during peak hours.

ending.debrief: Configuration Audit isn't just about catching extra, unapproved commits - it's equally about catching when prod is missing something the baseline requires. "Same feature, roughly" let an incident BL-02 existed specifically to prevent happen anyway.

check-nova-cache.speaker: You
check-nova-cache.narrative: CI 4 of 5: Nova Cache. Its baseline, BL-03, is tagged directly at prod's current commit.

c2.message: chore: tag baseline BL-03 - approved cache configuration

check-nova-cache.prompt: Does Nova Cache's prod still match its approved baseline?

choices.label: Yes - prod's commit ID is exactly BL-03's
No - can't be sure without comparing again

cache-flag-note.speaker: Narrator
cache-flag-note.narrative: You compare again anyway. They match exactly.

check-nova-gateway.speaker: You
check-nova-gateway.narrative: CI 5 of 5: Nova Gateway. Your audit log records BL-05 as approved at a specific commit: "chore: tag baseline BL-05 - approved gateway configuration." But the BL-05 ref right now points somewhere else entirely - at a later, unreviewed config tweak - and prod matches wherever BL-05 currently points.

g2.message: chore: tag baseline BL-05 - approved gateway configuration

check-nova-gateway.prompt: Does Nova Gateway's prod still match its approved baseline?

choices.label: No - prod matches where BL-05 points now, not the commit the audit log actually approved
Yes - prod's commit ID matches BL-05's tag exactly

gateway-pushback.speaker: Sana
gateway-pushback.narrative: "Matches the tag right now, sure - but a baseline tag isn't supposed to move after it's approved. Did you check what commit BL-05 was actually approved at, back when it was audited?"

gateway-escalate.speaker: You
gateway-escalate.narrative: "Matches the tag's current position" and "matches what was actually approved" stopped being the same claim the moment that tag moved.
gateway-escalate.prompt: Do you check the audit log's recorded commit, or defend matching the tag as good enough?

choices.label: Check the audit log's recorded commit for BL-05
Defend it - it matches the tag, that's what compliant means

gateway-worse.speaker: Narrator
gateway-worse.narrative: You sign off on Nova Gateway as compliant because it matches BL-05's tag. Nobody notices that the tag itself was quietly moved past a config tweak that never went through review.

gateway-bad-ending.speaker: Narrator
gateway-bad-ending.narrative: The retry-timeout tweak turns out to interact badly with a downstream service. By the time anyone traces it back, three more baselines have been "approved" the same unaudited way - by whatever the tag happened to point to.

ending.debrief: A baseline tag that can move after approval isn't a baseline - it's just a label. "Matches the tag" was never the same claim as "matches what the audit log actually approved," and treating them as identical let an unreviewed config change get retroactively blessed as part of BL-05.

resolution-clean.speaker: Narrator
resolution-clean.narrative: You catch Nova Gateway directly too: BL-05's tag now points to the retry-timeout tweak, not the commit the audit log actually recorded as approved. Five CIs checked: two genuinely drifted (Nova API's unaudited extra commit, Nova Worker's missing retry-cap fix), one baseline tag quietly moved past review (Nova Gateway), two actually compliant (Nova Web, Nova Cache). You close the quarterly audit with the real findings, not a wall of green checkmarks.

good-ending.speaker: Narrator
good-ending.narrative: The audit closes accurate. Nova API and Nova Worker get scheduled for proper review, and Nova Gateway's baseline gets re-pinned to a commit that's actually been through sign-off.

ending.debrief: Three different kinds of drift, caught the same way each time: by comparing an actual commit ID against what the audit log recorded as approved, not by trusting a tag's current position or a change's surface-level reasonableness. That's the whole discipline - Configuration Audit isn't about catching bad actors, it's about catching the moment "approved" quietly stops being true.

check-nova-gateway-b-late.speaker: Narrator
check-nova-gateway-b-late.narrative: You check the audit log directly. BL-05 was approved at the config-core commit - not the retry-timeout tweak the tag currently points to. You flag it.

resolution-recovered.speaker: Narrator
resolution-recovered.narrative: You get to the right call on all five CIs in the end. But it took Sana's question to catch that a moved baseline tag was still drift, just because it currently matches something.

neutral-ending.speaker: Narrator
neutral-ending.narrative: The quarterly audit closes accurate, corrected just before sign-off.

ending.debrief: You got there - but only because someone else asked whether a tag matching its own current position is the same as matching what was actually approved. It isn't. Catching that the first time, without needing the question asked back at you, is the habit a baseline's whole purpose depends on.
